title: Accounting as a Measurement Discipline – Valuation Principles, Accounting Estimates
outcomes: Explain the meaning of measurement and its three elements, and judge how far accounting is a measurement discipline.
Explain why money is an imperfect scale — not universal and not stable in dimension.
Measure an asset and a liability under historical cost, current cost, realisable value and present value, including discounting.
Explain accounting estimates, give examples and account for a change in estimate.

meta.exam_tip: Learn the four bases for both assets and liabilities, and practise one present-value computation with the annuity formula. Theory questions often ask "Is accounting a measurement discipline?".

concepts.title: Meaning of measurement and its three elements
body: Measurement is a vital part of accounting; transactions and events are measured mainly in money. Prof. R. J. Chambers described measurement as assigning numbers to objects and events by rules that specify the property being measured, the scale used and the dimension of the unit. Kohler described it as assigning ordinal or cardinal numbers to the results of an inquiry or observation following logical or mathematical rules.
Ordinal numbers show position in a sequence (first, second, third); cardinal numbers show how many (one, two, three). Accountants use cardinal numbers — rupee amounts.

From Chambers' definition, every measurement discipline has three elements: (1) identifying the objects and events to be measured, (2) selecting the standard or scale, and (3) evaluating the dimension (stability) of that standard or scale. These elements are used to judge how far accounting is a measurement discipline.
concepts.analogy: Measuring a room: decide what to measure (length of a wall), choose the scale (metres), and make sure the tape does not stretch (stable dimension).
concepts.work: Before valuing anything — an inventory, a business, a claim — a CA asks the same three questions: what exactly is being valued, in what unit, and can that unit be trusted over time?

concepts.title: Objects or events to be measured
body: Accounting identifies, measures and communicates economic information for decisions, so what it measures is information. Decision-makers need past, present and future information; external users are usually given past information.

There is no fixed set of objects and events: for cash management the relevant items are cash receipts and payments (past and projected); for a lender, the borrower's debt-servicing ability — past results, present position and projections.

Things that have already happened, or exist now, can be measured fairly accurately; future ones can only be predicted, not measured. Yet prediction is an essential part of accounting information because decisions concern the future.
concepts.analogy: A doctor uses your past reports (measured) and current tests (measured) to forecast your health next year (predicted).
concepts.work: Bank appraisal notes combine audited past figures with projected cash flows. A CA preparing projections must make clear which figures are measured facts and which are predictions.

concepts.title: Money as the scale — and its weaknesses
body: In accounting, money is the scale of measurement (money measurement concept); quantitative information is given only as a supplement.

Not universal: money has no single worldwide denomination — rupee in India, dollar in the USA, pound sterling in the UK — and exchange rates keep changing. A USD 10,000 loan recorded at ₹83 becomes ₹86 per dollar later; the same obligation now measures ₹8,60,000 instead of ₹8,30,000.

Not stable in dimension: an ideal scale does not change over time (a kilogram or a metre stays the same), but the purchasing power of money keeps changing with prices. Rupee figures of different years are therefore not strictly comparable — sales value may rise while the quantity sold falls.

concepts.analogy: Money is like a rubber ruler: it measures, but it stretches with inflation and is a different ruler in every country.
concepts.work: When presenting a five-year trend to a client, a CA often shows volumes alongside rupee figures, so that price rises are not mistaken for real growth.

concepts.title: Is accounting a measurement discipline?
body: Accounting measures performance (profit or loss) and position (balance sheet), and a set of assumptions governs that measurement — going concern, consistency and accrual are taken for granted as fundamental assumptions, and various policies are adopted.

But accounting is not an exact measurement discipline: its scale (money) is neither universal nor stable in dimension, and much of accounting — recording, classifying, summarising and communicating — lies outside measurement altogether. So we cannot simply call accounting a measurement discipline, though measurement is an important part of it. For our study we take it as given that transactions are recorded in money, with quantities as supplementary information.
concepts.analogy: A journalist measures some things (votes counted, temperatures), but most of the job is reporting and explaining. Accounting is similar.
concepts.work: Explaining to a client that accounts give "a" true and fair view, not "the" exact value of his business, is part of managing expectations — especially in disputes and valuations.

concepts.title: The four valuation principles
body: Historical cost: acquisition price — e.g. machine price plus installation. Liabilities at the proceeds received (a ₹5 lakh bank loan at ₹5 lakh), or for items like income tax, at the amount expected to be paid. Commonly used for long-term assets.
Current cost: what it would cost to acquire the same or an equivalent asset now; liabilities at the undiscounted amount needed to settle them now (including, say, a prepayment penalty).

Realisable (settlement) value: what an asset would fetch now in an orderly disposal (a hurried sale may fetch less); liabilities at the undiscounted amount expected to be paid in the normal course. Commonly applied to inventories (lower of cost and net realisable value).

Present value: the discounted value of future net cash inflows (assets) or outflows (liabilities) in the normal course of business — used for investments and loans. Because of the time value of money, ₹100 receivable a year later is worth less than ₹100 today; discounting uses P = A ÷ (1 + i)^n, and for an equal annual amount, PV = A/i × [1 − 1/(1 + i)^n].
The traditional system is called historical cost accounting, but in later CA studies you will see that all four bases are used; most transactions are still measured at historical cost.

concepts.analogy: Your old car: what you paid (historical cost), what a new one costs today (current cost), what a dealer would pay you (realisable value), and what the rides it will give you are worth in today's money (present value).
concepts.work: Valuation reports for mergers, insurance claims and lender security use different bases for different purposes. A CA must state clearly which basis is used and why.

concepts.title: Measurement and valuation
body: Value relates to the benefit to be derived from an object, ability or idea. To an economist, value is utility — the satisfaction a resource gives — often expressed on ordinal scales (more or less satisfying).

Accountants use a money surrogate and only cardinal scales: value is shown by measurement in money. When a car bought for ₹2,50,000 is recorded at that amount, it is only one kind of value — acquisition (historical) cost. So in accounting, valuation is always measurement in money terms using a chosen basis.
concepts.analogy: A painting may be "priceless" to its owner (economic value as satisfaction), but the accounts can only show a number in rupees — what was paid for it.
concepts.work: Clients often say "this machine is worth much more to us". A CA explains that the accounts carry it on a measurement basis (usually cost), not its subjective worth.

concepts.title: Accounting estimates
body: Some items have not yet happened and cannot be measured by a valuation principle, but must still be recorded — such as provision for doubtful debts. For them, reasonable estimates are made using the current situation and past experience, based on the latest information available.

Estimates are needed for depreciation and amortisation, impairment losses, accruals, provisions, employee benefit obligations, bad debts, useful life and residual value of plant, inventory obsolescence, the period of benefit from a patent, provisions for unforeseen contingencies on long-term contracts, and tax provisions where interpretations may differ.

An estimate may need revision when the circumstances on which it was based change, or new information, more experience or later developments become available. A change in accounting estimate is the difference between what was estimated earlier and what is re-estimated (or actually achieved) in the current period — e.g. a machine expected to last 10 years becomes obsolete after 3 and is now expected to last only 3 more years. The revised estimate is applied from the period of change; earlier figures are not reworked.

jobs.title: Which value goes into the report?
jobs.role: Article assistant helping with a valuation for a bank loan
jobs.situation: A client wants a loan against his plant. He offers the original invoice (₹40 lakh, 8 years old), a supplier quote for a new plant (₹75 lakh) and a dealer's offer to buy the used plant (₹28 lakh).
steps: Identify the bases: invoice = historical cost; supplier quote = current cost; dealer offer = realisable value.
Ask what the bank needs: security value if the loan goes bad — realisable value in an orderly sale is the relevant base.
Note that the client's books will still show the plant at historical cost less depreciation (going concern).
State the basis used and its source clearly in the report.
jobs.takeaway: There is no single "value" — each basis answers a different question. Always say which basis you used and why.
jobs.think: Why would the bank ignore the ₹75 lakh figure?
jobs.answer: Current cost tells what a new plant would cost to buy; the bank wants to know what it could recover by selling the existing plant, which is its realisable value.

jobs.title: Testing a doubtful-debt estimate
jobs.role: Audit assistant at a distribution company
jobs.situation: Management has provided 2% of receivables as doubtful, the same as every year. This year two large customers are 9 months overdue and one has filed for insolvency.
steps: Collect the ageing of receivables and recent recovery history.
Compare the estimate with the latest information — the insolvent customer and the long-overdue balances.
Recommend revising the estimate (specific provision for the insolvent customer plus a higher general rate if justified).
Record that the revision is a change in estimate, recognised in the current period.
jobs.takeaway: Estimates must use the latest information. "Same as last year" is not a reason when circumstances have changed.

mcqs.q: According to Chambers' definition, the three elements of measurement are identification of objects and events, selection of a standard or scale, and:
options: Evaluation of the dimension of the measurement scale
mcqs.explain: Chambers described measurement as having three elements: identifying the objects and events to be measured, selecting a standard or scale, and evaluating the dimension of that scale — that is, whether the unit stays stable. The tempting option, communication to users, is part of the definition of accounting, not of measurement. In practice: when an accountant measures a company's sales in rupees, the third element reminds her that a rupee in 2015 and a rupee in 2026 do not buy the same goods.

mcqs.q: Numbers that indicate position in an ordered sequence (first, second, third) are called:
mcqs.explain: Ordinal numbers show position in an ordered sequence — first, second, third — without telling us by how much one exceeds another. Cardinal numbers show 'how many' or 'how much', and accounting uses cardinal numbers such as ₹5,00,000 of sales. The trap is cardinal numbers, which measure quantity, not rank. In practice: an analyst who ranks companies by market share uses an ordinal scale, while the sales figures in each company's accounts are cardinal.

mcqs.q: Money is not an ideal scale of measurement mainly because:
options: Its purchasing power changes and it differs across countries
It cannot be added or subtracted
It is not accepted by banks
mcqs.explain: A good measurement scale should be universal and stable. Money fails both tests: its purchasing power changes with inflation, and different countries use different currencies whose exchange rates move. The tempting option, 'it cannot be added or subtracted', is false — money is easily added and subtracted, which is why it is used. In practice: an Indian company with subsidiaries abroad must translate dollar and euro figures into rupees, and the results change with exchange rates.

mcqs.q: The valuation principle commonly applied to inventories (lower of cost and net realisable value) involves:
mcqs.explain: Inventory is carried at whichever is smaller — its cost or its net realisable value. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell, so the realisable value basis comes into play whenever it falls below cost. The tempting option, present value, involves discounting future cash flows and is used mainly for investments and loans, not inventory. In practice: a mobile retailer values old models at net realisable value when a new launch forces it to sell them below cost.

mcqs.q: Present value of ₹1,21,000 receivable after 2 years, discounted at 10% a year, is:
mcqs.explain: Present value = Amount ÷ (1 + i)ⁿ = ₹1,21,000 ÷ (1.10)² = ₹1,21,000 ÷ 1.21 = ₹1,00,000. The tempting ₹1,10,000 discounts for only one year (₹1,21,000 ÷ 1.10), ignoring the second year. Money received later is worth less today because it could have earned interest meanwhile. In practice: banks and analysts discount future loan repayments or project cash flows in exactly this way to decide what they are worth today.

mcqs.q: A machine was bought for ₹5,00,000 plus freight ₹20,000 and installation ₹30,000. Its historical cost is:
mcqs.explain: Historical cost is the acquisition price plus all costs needed to bring the asset to its location and working condition: ₹5,00,000 + freight ₹20,000 + installation ₹30,000 = ₹5,50,000. The tempting ₹5,20,000 includes freight but leaves out installation; a machine cannot be used until it is installed, so installation is part of its cost. In practice: fixed asset registers in Indian companies record each machine at its full landed and installed cost.

mcqs.q: A liability carried at the undiscounted amount of cash that would be required to settle it today is measured at:
mcqs.explain: Under the current cost basis, liabilities are carried at the undiscounted amount of cash that would be needed to settle the obligation today. The tempting option, present value, would discount future payments — but the question says 'undiscounted', which rules it out. Historical cost would use the amount received when the obligation arose. In practice: current cost thinking appears when a business asks how much cash it would need today to settle its supplier dues or loans.

mcqs.q: A loan of USD 20,000 was recorded at ₹82 per dollar. At the year end the rate is ₹85. The rupee amount of the loan at the year-end rate is:
mcqs.explain: At the year-end rate, the loan is USD 20,000 × ₹85 = ₹17,00,000, compared with ₹16,40,000 (20,000 × ₹82) originally recorded. The tempting ₹16,40,000 is the old figure at the original rate. The ₹60,000 rise shows that money is not a universal, stable scale. In practice: Indian companies with foreign-currency loans restate them at the closing exchange rate each year and record the exchange difference.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an accounting estimate?
mcqs.explain: An accounting estimate is a judgement made where an amount cannot be measured exactly. The useful life of a machine depends on expected usage, wear and technology, so it is an estimate. Cash paid for rent, share capital issued and invoice values are facts that can be verified from documents. The trap is assuming every figure in the accounts is exact. In practice: management estimates useful lives, bad debt provisions and warranty costs every year, and auditors test whether they are reasonable.

mcqs.q: Machine cost ₹9,00,000, life 10 years, straight-line, no residual value. After 3 years the remaining life is revised to 4 years. Revised annual depreciation is:
mcqs.explain: Annual depreciation = ₹9,00,000 ÷ 10 = ₹90,000, so after 3 years the carrying amount is ₹9,00,000 − ₹2,70,000 = ₹6,30,000. A change in useful life is a change in estimate, applied from the year of change: ₹6,30,000 ÷ 4 = ₹1,57,500 a year. The tempting ₹2,25,000 (₹9,00,000 ÷ 4) ignores the depreciation already charged. In practice: companies revise remaining lives when engineers report faster wear, and do not restate past years.

mcqs.q: The present value basis is most commonly used in accounting for:
mcqs.explain: The present value basis discounts future cash flows to today, so it suits items whose value lies in future receipts or payments — investments and loans. The tempting option, inventories, is carried at cost or realisable value, whichever is smaller, not at present value. Petty cash and share capital are recorded at face amounts. In practice: banks measure loans and bond investments using discounted cash flows, and long-term receivables are often discounted.

mcqs.q: To an economist, value means utility (satisfaction). In accounting, value is:
options: Measured in money using a cardinal scale
Expressed on an ordinal scale of satisfaction
mcqs.explain: An economist sees value as utility, which can only be ranked (ordinal). Accounting cannot measure satisfaction directly, so it uses money as a substitute and records value on a cardinal scale, such as historical cost in rupees. The tempting option, 'always the current market price', is wrong because accounting commonly uses historical cost, not market price. In practice: a company's balance sheet shows its office building at cost less depreciation, not at what it is worth to the owners.

mcqs.q: Present value of ₹50,000 a year for 3 years at 10% (rounded to the nearest rupee) is:
mcqs.explain: Present value of an annuity = Annual amount × [1 − (1.10)⁻³] ÷ 0.10 = ₹50,000 × 2.48685 = ₹1,24,343 (rounded). The tempting ₹1,50,000 simply adds the three receipts and ignores the time value of money. The figure is also less than ₹1,36,364, which wrongly discounts all three receipts for only one year. In practice: lease liabilities and long-term instalment receivables are measured in Indian accounts by discounting a series of payments like this.

questions.q: Meridian Ltd bought a machine some years ago for ₹15,00,000 and paid freight ₹75,000 and installation ₹25,000. It also has a 10% loan of ₹4,00,000 repayable in 3 years. Today: an equivalent machine would cost ₹22,00,000; the machine could be sold in an orderly sale for ₹12,00,000; it will generate net cash inflows of ₹3,00,000 a year for 4 years; the lender would accept immediate repayment with a 1% penalty; the discount rate is 10%. Value the machine and the loan under the four valuation principles.

questions.q: "Accounting is not an exact measurement discipline." Discuss with reference to the elements of measurement.

model.text: Chambers defines measurement as assigning numbers to objects and events by rules that specify the property, the scale and the dimension of the unit. Its three elements are: identification of objects and events, selection of a standard or scale, and evaluation of the dimension of that scale.

items: Objects and events: accounting measures information for decisions. Past and present items can be measured with some accuracy, but future events, which decisions depend on, can only be predicted.
Scale: money is the scale, but it has no universal denomination (rupee, dollar, pound) and exchange rates fluctuate — a foreign-currency loan measures differently at different dates.

Dimension: an ideal scale is stable (a kilogram is always a kilogram); money's purchasing power changes with prices, so figures of different years are not truly comparable — sales value can rise while quantity falls.

Also, much of accounting — recording, classifying, summarising and communicating — is not measurement at all, and measurement rests on assumptions (going concern, consistency, accrual) and chosen policies.

model.text: Hence measurement is an important part of accounting, but accounting is not an exact measurement discipline.

questions.q: What are accounting estimates? Give four situations where estimates are needed, and explain what a change in accounting estimate means.

model.text: Some items cannot be measured precisely because they depend on uncertain future events, yet they must be recorded. Management therefore makes reasonable estimates of assets, liabilities, income and expenses using the latest information, the existing situation and past experience — for example, provision for doubtful debts.

items: Useful life and residual value of plant (depreciation) and period of benefit of a patent (amortisation).
Provision for doubtful debts and inventory obsolescence.
Provisions for warranties, employee benefits and unforeseen contingencies on long-term contracts.
Provision for taxes where tax authorities may interpret items differently.

model.text: A change in accounting estimate is the difference between a figure estimated earlier and its re-estimate, or the actual result, in the current period — caused by changed circumstances, new information or more experience. Example: a machine expected to last 10 years becomes obsolete and is now expected to last only 3 more years; depreciation is revised from the period of change.

summary: Measurement (Chambers): numbers assigned to objects/events by rules specifying property, scale and dimension. Elements: objects/events, standard or scale, dimension of the scale.
Money is the scale: not universal (currencies, exchange rates) and not stable in dimension (purchasing power) — accounting is not an exact measurement discipline.
Four bases: historical cost, current cost, realisable (settlement) value, present value — each defined for assets and for liabilities.
Value to the economist = utility (ordinal); to the accountant = money measure (cardinal).
Estimates (doubtful debts, useful life, obsolescence, warranties, tax) use latest information; changes in estimate are applied from the period of change.
remember: P = A ÷ (1 + i)^n; annuity PV = A/i × [1 − 1/(1 + i)^n].
Historical cost of an asset includes freight and installation.
Inventories — lower of cost and NRV; investments and loans — present value; long-term assets — historical cost.
traps: Current cost of a liability is undiscounted (includes any penalty to settle now).
Present value of a loan = PV of interest + PV of principal.
A change in useful life is a change in estimate, not in accounting policy.

viva.model: Money is not a perfect scale because it is not universal — every country has its own currency and exchange rates keep changing — and it is not stable in dimension, because its purchasing power changes with prices, so figures of different years are not comparable.

viva.q: Name and explain the four valuation principles.
viva.model: The four valuation principles are historical cost, which is the acquisition price paid; current cost, which is what it would cost to acquire the same or an equivalent asset now; realisable value, which is what the asset would fetch now in an orderly sale; and present value, which is the discounted value of the future net cash flows.

viva.q: Explain the present value basis with the idea of time value of money.
viva.model: Under the present value basis, an asset is carried at the discounted value of the future net cash inflows it will generate, and a liability at the discounted value of the future cash outflows needed to settle it. It is based on the time value of money: a rupee received in future is worth less than a rupee today, so future amounts are discounted using P equals A divided by one plus i to the power n.

viva.q: What are accounting estimates, and what is meant by a change in estimate?
viva.model: Accounting estimates are reasonable judgements made for items that cannot be measured precisely because they depend on uncertain future events, such as provision for doubtful debts, useful life of machinery or inventory obsolescence. A change in estimate arises when an earlier estimate is revised because of new information, changed circumstances or more experience, for example when the remaining useful life of a machine is reduced.

viva.q: Is accounting an exact measurement discipline?
viva.model: No, accounting is not an exact measurement discipline. Its scale, money, is neither universal nor stable in dimension, future events can only be predicted, and much of accounting such as recording, classifying, summarising and communicating is not measurement at all, although measurement is an important part of it.

cases.title: Harbour Logistics — valuing a crane
cases.case: Harbour Logistics bought a crane on 1 April 2022 for ₹24,00,000 and paid ₹1,00,000 for installation. It was depreciated on the straight-line basis over 10 years with no residual value. On 1 April 2026: a new equivalent crane costs ₹32,00,000; the old crane could be sold in an orderly sale for ₹17,00,000; it is expected to produce net cash inflows of ₹5,00,000 a year for the next 5 years; and the discount rate is 10%. Engineers also say that, because of heavy use, the crane will last only 3 more years instead of 6.

mcqs.q: What is the historical cost of the crane?
mcqs.explain: Historical cost is the purchase price plus costs needed to bring the asset into use: ₹24,00,000 + installation ₹1,00,000 = ₹25,00,000. The tempting ₹32,00,000 is the cost of a new equivalent crane today — that is current cost, not historical cost. Later price changes do not alter the historical cost recorded. In practice: a logistics company's fixed asset register keeps each crane at its original installed cost, while current cost is used only for insurance or replacement planning.

mcqs.q: What is the present value of the expected inflows (to the nearest rupee)?
mcqs.explain: Present value of ₹5,00,000 a year for 5 years at 10% = ₹5,00,000 × [1 − (1.10)⁻⁵] ÷ 0.10 = ₹5,00,000 × 3.79079 = ₹18,95,393. The tempting ₹25,00,000 adds the five years' inflows without discounting; money received in year five is worth much less today. In practice: valuers compute value in use exactly this way when testing whether an asset is impaired.

mcqs.q: The ₹17,00,000 the crane could fetch in an orderly sale represents which basis?
mcqs.explain: Realisable value is the amount that could be obtained now by selling the asset in an orderly disposal — here ₹17,00,000. The tempting option, current cost, is the ₹32,00,000 needed to buy an equivalent new crane today; it is a buying price, while realisable value is a selling price. In practice: lenders financing equipment look at realisable value when deciding how much security an asset provides if the borrower defaults.

mcqs.q: After revising the remaining life to 3 years, the annual depreciation from 2026-27 is:
mcqs.explain: Annual depreciation was ₹25,00,000 ÷ 10 = ₹2,50,000; after 4 years (2022-23 to 2025-26) the carrying amount is ₹25,00,000 − ₹10,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. Revising the remaining life is a change in estimate applied prospectively: ₹15,00,000 ÷ 3 = ₹5,00,000 a year. The tempting ₹2,50,000 keeps the old charge, ignoring the revised life. In practice: past years are not restated; only current and future depreciation changes.
